newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right says Jospin punishes firms, hits jobs.
newsitem.headline: French right says Jospin punishes firms, hits jobs.

text.p: France's right-wing opposition hit out at corporate tax rises unveiled by the leftist government on Monday to qualify for a single European Union currency, saying they would punish companies and jack up unemployment.

"At the end of the day, these measures will lead to less investment, fewer jobs and lower wages," said former finance minister Alain Madelin, a free-marketeer and head of the opposition Liberal Democracy party.

The Socialist-led government's Communist junior partners and trade union allies praised the measures to cut the 1997 budget deficit, estimated to be running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, while avoiding raising taxes on households.
Seeking to put the deficit back on track for the EU's Maastricht Treaty goal of three percent of GDP, the government announced new taxes and savings representing 0.4 percentage points of GDP.
It plans to raise an extra 22 billion francs ($3.6 billion) by additional taxes on larger firms' profits and capital gains, and save 10 billion francs in spending cuts.

Right-wingers blasted Prime Minister Lionel Jospin for penalising companies, noting he also expected the private sector to create 350,000 jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.
But political commentators said the opposition was on shaky ground because the centre-right government defeated on June 1 had not revealed the true size of the deficit.

"The economic choices of this government go against the liberal policies which, throughout the world, allow growth and employment via cuts in state spending, lower taxes and privatisations," Madelin said.
"You can't be part of the euro game by swimming against the European tide," he said.
Former foreign minister Herve de Charette, like Madelin a member of the centre-right Union for French Democracy umbrella group, said "one series of fiscal measures may conceal another".
"For the time being, (the government) is weakening companies and penalising jobs but it is hiding its true choices. I strongly fear that the worst is yet to come," he said.
The CAC-40 index of the Paris bourse was down 0.7 percent in late trading.

Philippe Auberger, a parliamentary budget expert for President Jacques Chirac's conservative Gaullist RPR party, said: "The government is asking companies to make an extra effort (in taxes) while expecting them to hire more young people. That seems completely contradictory to me."

The extreme-right National Front said the measures proved that mainstream politicians had no answers. "The audit demanded by Lionel Jospin proves at least one thing: left or right, they are equally bad managers," it said.
The left-leaning daily Le Monde said in an editorial that Jospin's choices were a "flagrant rebuttal" of those who said left-right economic policy differences had vanished in France.
It was "the first time for ages that a Socialist government has refused to attack the middle classes, even the best off among them. This is a strong -- and good -- political choice."

France's biggest trade union, the Socialist-led CFDT, which supports the euro, hailed the government plan as a "balanced choice between the necessary reduction of deficits and the resumption of economic activity".
